Excellent essay!

One gap is that the firm solves a third problem: assurance that the work gets done.

Employment contracts buy the right to direct labor within limits, an option on effort. 

In open source, maintenance is where things get slippery. Is it the case that peer production and contributions have been subsidized by wage-paying firms that covered core builds (e.g., kernels)?

But that's a minor quibble.
content_html:
The Post-Coasean Firm

One of my earlier predictions from a lifetime ago (six months) was that AI will require a re-thinking of Coase’s theory of the firm. Economist Ronald Coase’s question in The Nature of the Firm written in 1937 was why do firms exist when markets are capable of coordinating economic activity through prices? His answer was that market transactions themselves have costs. Someone has to discover accurate prices, identify counterparties, negotiate contracts, monitor performance, and continually renegotiate arrangements as circumstances change. At some point, instead of negotiating every single transaction, it becomes cheaper to bring a set of activities under a common organization, where a manager can direct resources without negotiating a new market contract for every task. Rephrased in the age of AI, if you and I have agents that can co-ordinate with each other and other agents to accurately price our goods and services, why should firms exist at all? If artificial intelligence reduces the cost of finding information, writing code, drafting contracts, monitoring activity, and assigning work, then it should reduce transaction costs. The boundaries of firms should become more porous. We should have fewer managers. Small teams should be able to coordinate capacities themselves. Activities once internalized by companies could be negotiated with the market by agents. The firm might begin to dissolve into a network of transactions, all managed by agents. All of us would be liberated from the perceived tyranny of management. Some of this is clearly happening. It is considerably easier to ask an agent to negotiate a refund, research a purchase, produce a small application, or perform a sequence of administrative tasks. Twitter is chokeful of people talking about how they got their AI agent to get them a refund or more credit card points. But inside actual organizations the effect is much less clean. A firm in which everyone can generate software and writing probably experiences more coordination overhead rather than less. Even seasoned AI promoters like the CEO of Shopify, Tobi Lutke, have started talking about people in organizations becoming slop grenades. To understand what’s happening, we should go back to Coase’s original thesis about what makes firms necessary and some pre-history of how “management” became a job.

From transaction costs to managerial coordination

The boundary of the firm is determined by the comparative costs of two forms of coordination. On one side is coordination through contracts and prices, and on the other is coordination through administration. Coase’s idea is that firms solve for transaction costs by moving activity inside the boundary of the firm. But, once activities have been moved inside the firm, how are they actually coordinated? Alfred Chandler attempts to answer this in his book The Visible Hand (1980). According to Chandler, who is a technical historian, prior to 1840, US business mostly consisted of small merchants who managed their own firms. There was some specialization that had happened in accounting and other aspects, but by and large it was business as usual. What changed things was the introduction of railroads. If a railroad had a number of parallel tracks and ran few trains on each, the need for intensive managerial coordination would not have been great. But if the substantial costs of multiple tracking and nonintensive use of the tracks were to be avoided without disastrous safety consequences, substantial managerial input was imperative. Most railroads adopted single tracks because it provided the right trade off between price of physical capital (building several lines) and managerial services. The result of this decision was the appearance in the 1850s of a new phenomenon – the managerial firm in which managers supervised not only workers but also other layers of managers. These managers soon developed many of the basic tools essential for modern management. The line staff organization was developed by the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1857. Most of the techniques of modern accounting beyond double-entry bookkeeping were invented in the period between 1850 and 1870. Other factors such as increasing competition between the firms led to the expansion of the managerial class. For example, as movement of freight through rail became popular, it became more important for firms to co-ordinate with each other to ensure that goods traveling lines serviced by different railroads actually made it to its final location without being held up. This required a huge overhead of clerks stationed in various locations. It is also interesting to note that these firms were extremely large for their time. The Pennsylvania Railroad employed three times more people than the United States army in the 1870s. Railroads also played a more extended role in Chandler’s early history of management. Since they were the biggest and most successful companies of their time, railroad companies’ new organization methods became models for other industries, and institutions created to support railroads such as the modern stock market, later served other firms as well. Secondly, and perhaps more important as an analogy for our current times, the speed and reliability of railroads changed how companies thought about inventory and production. When materials were transported through waterways, it was slower and affected by seasonalities, but now you could accurately know when you got materials in production and out for delivery, and this meant that firms hired more managers to make their production more efficient. Essentially, the speed of the railways caused a co-ordination bottleneck at the factories, which was solved by the new managerial class.

Integration and the architecture of complexity

Railroads were followed by other technologies that reduced the practical distance between organizations such as the telegraph, telephone, radio, and eventually computers. If every increase in communication speed had simply required another layer of managers to absorb the resulting coordination burden, the modern economy would have ended up buried under a kafkaesque bureacracy. Some parts of it arguably did. But another way of handling complexity was to make components of a firm more decomposable. In  The Architecture of Complexity, Herbert Simon argues that complex systems remain manageable because they are nearly decomposable. Their parts are not independent, but interactions within a subsystem are much more frequent and consequential than interactions between subsystems. A department can therefore do most of its work without constantly consulting every other department, or a component in a machine can be changed without redesigning the entire machine. In Simon’s terms, the system works because most activity is local, while interactions between modules are comparatively limited. That means the boundary between modules matters enormously. A nearly decomposable system needs some way for its subsystems to communicate without exposing all of their internal complexity to one another. The interface specifies what has to cross the boundary while allowing everything behind it to remain relatively autonomous. We are now very familiar with a software version of this argument through the popularization of APIs and now MCPs that provide interfaces into other systems and apps. Decomposability therefore reduces integration costs by limiting both the amount and the kind of information that has to move between subsystems. To continue on the railroad analogy used by Chandler, we can look at containerization in the shipping industry to understand what happens when we create nearly decomposable interfaces between systems. As Marc Levinson describes in The Box, conventional freight moved as breakbulk cargo. Barrels, sacks, crates, machinery, bundles of lumber, and other goods arrived at the waterfront separately. Longshoremen had to handle them piece by piece: move them from truck or warehouse to the pier, sort them, check them against manifests, lift them into the ship, and find an appropriate place to stow each item in the hold. At the destination, essentially the same process happened in reverse. Ships could spend days or even weeks in port, and the physical handoff between land and sea transportation was expensive, slow, prone to theft and damage, and dependent on large amounts of local knowledge and labor. Contemporary estimates cited in discussions of Levinson’s account put port activity at a majority of the total cost of sea transport in the late 1950s. The inefficiency was concentrated at the boundary between systems. Trucks were good at moving goods over roads and ships were good at moving them over oceans, but transferring cargo between the two required opening up the contents of one transportation system and reconstructing them inside another. Every shipment arrived at the boundary in a different form. Integration required people to inspect and reorganize the cargo itself. The shipping container changed that relationship. Instead of making the trucker, port, ship, railroad, and warehouse coordinate around the particular contents of every shipment, they could coordinate around a standardized box. Cargo could be packed once near its origin and then moved as a single unit from truck to ship to rail and back again. Cranes could lift the same standardized object regardless of what was inside it. The internal organization of the cargo became largely irrelevant to the next transportation subsystem. What mattered were the container’s specifications. This produced enormous savings in loading time and port labor. One account drawing on Levinson contrasts breakbulk loading costs of $5.86 per ton in 1956 with roughly sixteen cents per ton for containerized loading. And downstream of that, ships no longer had to spend much of their useful life sitting in port while thousands of individual objects were reconciled between transportation systems. The container therefore embedded an interface into the physical infrastructure of trade. In Simon’s terms, containerization made freight transportation more nearly decomposable. It reduced the information that had to cross the boundary between transportation systems by making that boundary more rigid and predictable. Complexity did not disappear; much of it moved to either side of the interface. This also changed the organizational possibilities available to firms. Chandler’s railroads had responded to coordination problems largely by bringing activities under common managerial control. Containerization showed that another solution was possible: standardize the interface strongly enough and the modules on either side of it can remain organizationally separate. Integration can be achieved through architecture rather than hierarchy. That gives us a more precise version of the Coasean problem. The firm exists partly because certain transactions are cheaper to coordinate internally, but internalization generates its own integration costs. Firms can manage those costs through managerial hierarchy, as Chandler showed, or reduce them by decomposing activity into modules connected by stable interfaces. The better those interfaces become, the more autonomy each module can sustain without forcing the rest of the system to understand how it works.

Open source and the partial disappearance of management

But what happens if we have technologies that can reduce integration costs even further? Yochai Benkler’s Coase’s Penguin begins from an apparent anomaly in Coase’s two-part world of markets and firms. Open Source projects such as Linux coordinate enormous amounts of productive activity without relying primarily on either prices or managerial commands. Contributors choose their own tasks, often without employment contracts or a centralized assignment. Benkler argues that networked production can outperform both markets and firms under certain conditions. Work must be sufficiently modular (and hence decomposable) that people can contribute independently. Tasks must exist at different levels of granularity so participants can contribute different amounts of effort. And the cost of integrating these contributions must remain low enough that decentralized participation does not generate more coordination overhead than it saves. Open source demonstrates that the allocation of work can be decentralized much further than the traditional firm suggests. Contributors can self-select into tasks using local knowledge about their interests, skills, and available time. You don’t really need a manager to match the right person to the right problem if there is sufficient motivation. But integration does not disappear with managerial allocation. Projects still require maintainers, interfaces, coding standards and review processes for deciding which contributions become part of the canonical project. Fred Turner and his collaborators make this point in their critique of expansive theories of peer production. Peer production may look spontaneous from the outside, but it rests on structural and cultural scaffolding. Simply put, the disappearance of a conventional boss does not imply the disappearance of hierarchy, authority, rules, or institutional design.

The jagged Coasean frontier

Generative AI pushes Benkler’s experiment further because it lowers the cost of contribution in several different ways at once. A worker no longer has to begin with a blank document or codebase. An agent can search for relevant information, break a problem into subtasks, produce candidate solutions, call tools, and in some cases pass work to other agents. Tasks that once justified going through a manager, hiring a contractor, or waiting for another department can increasingly be attempted directly. For relatively isolated tasks, this looks a lot like the Coasean prediction. Getting a refund is a good example. The objective and relevant information required is narrow, and success can usually be easily recognized. If an agent can read the policy, communicate with the merchant, and negotiate the refund, several transaction costs really have disappeared. The same is true of many small programming jobs. If I need a script to transform one file format into another, the output can often be tested locally and accepted or discarded without affecting very much else. The effect changes once the task has a large integration surface. Suppose an employee uses AI to redesign a customer-support workflow. Producing the workflow may now be cheap. But putting it into operation means establishing how it interacts with the customer database, permissions, reporting, legal requirements and the responsibilities of other teams. Someone also has to make the final call on whether the new workflow replaces the old one, whether both should coexist, and which version becomes authoritative. You might still need to train people on the new system. The work of producing a candidate solution has become easier while the work of making that solution part of the firm has not disappeared. You can see similar dynamics play out in other fields involving knowledge work. A couple of weeks ago there was uproar about the essay Math and AI signed by several field medalists. People were arguing whether the field of esoteric math proofs was worth preserving, but this missed the point. The core argument raised by the essay was that you can spend a lot of money to generate proofs, but if no one understands what has been proven, then the proof is essentially useless. In other words, if the proof is not integrated with the knowledge ecosystem of maths, then it will just be another benchmark for AI models and nothing more. In creative markets, cheap generation can make it much easier to imitate a successful game mechanic or visual style without making the exploratory work that discovered the mechanic any easier. What becomes cheap in each case is different, but the pattern is similar: one stage of production accelerates faster than the institutions that select, interpret, or incorporate its outputs. AI therefore changes transaction costs unevenly. Search, decomposition, drafting, and local execution can become dramatically cheaper while verification, integration, judgment, and authority remain comparatively expensive. In some cases those downstream costs increase simply because the number of candidate actions has grown. This is the sense in which the Coasean frontier is jagged. Within the firm, different parts of the production process are becoming cheaper at different rates. Benkler’s open-source example anticipated part of this problem. Peer production could decentralize the allocation of work because contributors could self-select into modular tasks. But Linux still required maintainers to decide what entered the kernel.

Integration regimes

If AI lowers the cost of producing work, then the remaining management problem is deciding how that work gets integrated. Some kinds of work can be made explicit enough that a system can evaluate them through rules. Other kinds still depend on interpretation. The first question is how formalized the interface is. By this I mean how much of the relevant work can be expressed in a form that a machine can act on. An API is a simple example. It describes what information a system will accept and what operations another system can request. The internal workings of both sides can remain hidden because the interaction between them has been reduced to a stable interface. MCP builds on the same logic for AI systems. It gives a model a structured way to discover tools and understand what actions are available. The model can then invoke those tools through a defined interface. A computational expression that a machine can act on need not necessarily be as smart as an AI. There are less technical examples we deal with on a daily basis. A permissions system specifies who can perform which actions. A database schema defines what kinds of objects a system recognizes. Automated tests specify some of the conditions a software contribution must satisfy. Procurement workflows encode when a purchase needs further approval. Each of these takes some part of an organizational decision and makes it computationally legible. The same logic appears in containerization. The shipping company, railroad, and trucking company could remain independently managed because the handoff between them had been formalized around the container. The interface constrained what had to be known about the other system. The relevant question for managers is can the conditions for a valid contribution be stated clearly enough that they can be checked computationally? But many activities can only be partially expressed in computation. You could have a Claude skill to do developmental edits on your essay, but there will be a gap between what is expressed in the skill and your own taste. This is where the second question comes in: where does authority over integration sit? Some systems distribute that authority widely because the interface itself does most of the work. Others concentrate authority in a manager, editor, maintainer, or specialist because the relevant judgment remains difficult to formalize. That gives us four broad integration regimes:

|
| Distributed authority | Concentrated authority | | --- | --------------------- | ---------------------- | | Low formalization | Exploratory peer production: contributors coordinate through norms, discussion, and reputation | Expert judgment: a founder, editor, principal investigator, or maintainer decides what belongs | | High formalization | Protocol-governed production: contributors act independently through explicit interfaces and validation rules | Bureaucratic or verified production: procedures are explicit, but designated authorities control approval and exceptions |

A young research group may sit in the low-formalization, concentrated-authority quadrant. The principal investigator cannot specify in advance what a good research direction will look like. The work depends on accumulated judgment. An informal open-source community may sit closer to low-formalization, distributed-authority. People choose their own problems and coordinate through discussion. Reputation and norms do a lot of heavy lifting here. As the project grows, this arrangement often becomes harder to sustain. More of the integration problem gets moved into tests, contribution rules, maintainership, and module boundaries. A mature protocol belongs closer to high-formalization, distributed-authority. Participants can act independently because the interface has already defined enough of the interaction. APIs, container standards, etc. are examples. Parts of open-source software also work this way once interfaces and tests become stable. The high-formalization, concentrated-authority quadrant is common in financial controls and regulated processes. The rules are explicit, but a designated authority still decides whether an action is permitted. Exceptions are handled centrally. The process can be highly computational while authority remains concentrated. The point of the matrix is that a complex organization has subsystems that are situated in different parts of this quadrant at any given time. A product team may depend heavily on taste and local judgment. A payments system benefits from strict interfaces. An experimental software branch can tolerate loose rules. A production branch may require tests and restricted merge permissions. The same module can also move between regimes over time. A new problem may begin in the judgment quadrant because nobody yet knows how to specify the decision rule. An expert decides case by case. Over time, patterns become visible. Some of that judgment can then be turned into tests, schemas, checklists, or protocols. Once that happens, authority can spread. Contributors no longer need access to all of the tacit knowledge that originally made the decision possible. They can act independently because the interface now carries part of that knowledge. AI increases the importance of this movement because it makes variation cheap. A research group can generate more hypotheses. An engineering team can generate more implementations. An operations team can generate more workflows. An open-source project can receive more patches. That increase in output raises a management question for each module: how much of the integration problem can be expressed computationally? Where the answer is “a lot,” AI can support much more autonomy. Agents can operate through existing APIs, tests, schemas, and permissions. They can produce work and have much of that work evaluated without continuous managerial attention. Where the answer is “not much,” the bottleneck remains judgment and leadership. Someone still has to decide and own whether a contribution is useful, whether an exception is justified, or whether the rules themselves need to change. This gives the two axes a practical interpretation. Formalization measures how much of the integration problem has been made computationally explicit. Authority concentration measures how much leadership and judgment is needed. As AI makes contribution cheaper, managers will have to make that distinction repeatedly. Which parts of a process can be turned into interfaces and protocols? Which parts still require someone to interpret the situation? And when should a module move from one regime to another?
